background.definition: Epistaxis is defined as any active bleeding from the nose.

list.listitem: Traces of blood from the nose were reported by 16.5% of female subjects of a telephone survey, and 7.6% reported significant bleeding within the preceding year.
There are 1.7 emergency department (ED) visits per 1000 US residents per year; 6% of those visits ended in hospitalization.
Incidence peaks in young children and again in the elderly. Epistaxis is more common in the winter.
Epistaxis accounts for approximately 1 in 200 visits to US EDs.

Local factors: nose picking, cold/dry air, trauma, nasal septal deviation, foreign bodies, nasal surgery, sinusitis, allergic rhinitis, chemical irritants (smoke), tumors, polyps, topical steroids, and vascular malformation.
Systemic causes: medications (eg, anticoagulants, aspirin, NSAIDs), platelet dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathies, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, and leukemia.

Atrophic rhinosinusitis is a chronic condition resulting from atrophy of the nasal mucosa and underlying bone that is characterized by thick, foul smelling discharge and thick dry crusts. It is associated with bacterial colonization and seen in warmer climates. It can also be associated with previous sinonasal surgery or sarcoidosis.

It is common lore for patients with nosebleeds to fear that they have hypertension. In a survey of more than 300 consecutive adults with hypertension, although there was no clear association between epistaxis and hypertension, there was a link between epistaxis and the duration of and presence of left ventricular hypertrophy, suggesting that epistaxis may be a consequence of long-standing hypertension.

Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) is a rare cause of frequent epistaxis. Incidence is between 1/3,500 and 1/40,000. Patients with this autosomal-dominant disease most often present with epistaxis but also have telangiectasias elsewhere on the skin and on internal organs.
More than 90% of bleeding is from the Kiesselbach plexus in the anterior, inferior aspect of the nasal septum.
Less than 10% of bleeding is from the posterior nasal cavity.
Bleeding from the superior nasal cavity is rare.
Moisturizing ambient air and avoiding nasal trauma (nose-picking) may decrease incidence of epistaxis. B
Petroleum jelly is ineffective in preventing recurrent epistaxis in children. B
A systematic review of preventive strategies (vaseline, antiseptic cream) found no conclusive results. B
Coagulation tests for epistaxis are not useful unless the patient is on an anticoagulant. B
Ask about medication use, especially anti-platelet agents and anticoagulants. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Extensive, sustained bleeding; other bleeding history
Chronic, thick, foul-smelling discharge; thick crusts

list.listitem: Diagnosis of epistaxis is usually straightforward, based on visible blood coming from the nares.
Occasionally, with a posterior bleed or supine patient, the blood can be swallowed and vomited.
The source of the hemorrhage should be identified by direct visualization. Examination is made easier with a good light source, nasal speculum, bayonet forceps, and suction.
Additional history may help to uncover the underlying cause of the bleeding (see Differential diagnosis table).

Symptoms of atrophic rhinosinusitis include fetor, crusting/nasal obstruction, epistaxis, anosmia and secondary infection. It is usually found in lower socioeconomic groups living in warm climates or in those with previous sinonasal surgery or sarcoidosis.

In a study of 144 patients seen in the ED for nosebleeds, 121 (86%) had coagulation studies. Only 8 patients had laboratory abnormalities, all of whom were taking warfarin or warfarin plus aspirin. Routine coagulation studies (PT, PTT, and platelet count) are not recommended for evaluation of epistaxis unless the patient is on anticoagulation or reports other episodes of bleeding that could indicate a coagulopathy.

In a study of a referral population of 248 children with epistaxis, 47 failed medical therapy, needed surgical nasal cautery, and received hematologic evaluation . Five patients were found to have some type of bleeding disorder: 3 with type 1 von Willebrand's disease, 1 with platelet aggregation disorder, and 1 with mild factor VII deficiency.

Once a vessel hemorrhages, it tends to do so repeatedly until it completely heals. In addition, because risk factors (eg, nose-picking, dry air) tend to be stable, repeated episodes of epistaxis do not necessarily require workup.
See for a suggested approach to management.
Simple measures are helpful in stopping most nosebleeds: nose blowing to clear clots, pinching the nose for 5-15 minutes and topical decongestants. C
In patients hospitalized for epistaxis, hot-water irrigation was as effective as tamponade but was significantly less painful and reduced length of stay by 1 day. B
Cauterizing visible bleeding vessels with AgNO3 or electrocautery is equally effective. B

Anterior packing with different nasal tampons appears to be equally effective. B Authors of a systematic review found that the Rapid Rhino and FloSeal packs may be better tolerated and easier to place.
Patients with resistant or posterior bleeds are likely to need posterior packing, surgery, arterial ligation, or embolization. C
Topical nasal decongestants can slow or stop bleeding. Useful agents include oxymetazoline and phenylephrine.

Topical analgesics such as tetracaine or lidocaine can make coagulation or packing more tolerable. Four percent cocaine can cause analgesia and vasoconstriction but is inconvenient to obtain and store.

In children with recurrent epistaxis, 55% of those treated with a topical antiseptic cream containing chlorhexidine and neomycin (not available in the United States) had no further bleeding in the next 4 weeks compared with only 29% of control patients (NNT = 4; 95% CI, 3-9).
Adding silver nitrate to topical antiseptic creams provided no additional benefit in treating recurrent epistaxis.

Prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin, cephalexin) are often used with nasal packing to prevent infection. A before-and-after study and a metanalysis failed to support this practice and showed a very low rate of infection in all groups.
Topical or oral tranexamic acid may reduce the rate of rebleeding. Topical tranexamic acid may also help stop bleeding.
Reversal of anticoagulation is indicated in patients with life-threatening epistaxis.
In patients with epistaxis caused by hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, intranasal bevacizumab, estriol, and tranexamic acid 10% were all no better than placebo.
High-quality studies comparing different procedures are lacking. A Cochrane review found only 5 small studies at high risk of bias.

Cauterizing visible bleeders with AgNO3 or electrocautery is equally effective. If using silver nitrate, use 75% rather than 95%, which is at least as effective and much less painful. Cauterize first around the bleeding site, then on it. Avoid cautery if the bleeding site cannot be clearly seen.

When silver nitrate cautery is used, it should only be applied briefly (about 5 seconds or less) and used for small areas of bleeding. Intranasal application of mixture of 1:1 phenylephrine and 4% viscous lidocaine prior to cautery can help dry the area and provide some anesthesia.

Practice guidelines from the American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation recommended using resorbable packing for patients with suspected bleeding disorder or for patients who are using anticoagulation or antiplatelet medications. They did not feel that a nasal clip had significant advantages over manual compression.
In patients hospitalized for epistaxis, hot-water irrigation was as effective as tamponade, was significantly less painful, and reduced length of stay by 1 day.
Hemostatic packing: absorbable gelatin foam or oxidized cellulose can be used if nasal tampons are not available.

Nasal packing : lubricate a nasal tampon with antibiotic ointment and insert. It expands on contact with fluid, tamponading the bleeding. Packing should be removed within 2 to 3 days. Balloon devices for this purpose are also available.
Careful placement of a trimmed foley catheter or a commercial nasal catheter may tamponade posterior bleeds.

For prevention of bleeding after endoscopic sinus surgery, there was no significant difference in pain and wound healing between polyvinyl alcohol-coated nasal packing and non-absorbable nasal packing in one small RCT.
In a study of only 19 patients, intranasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation was associated with shorter hospitalizations and greater patient satisfaction than conventional nasal packing.
Approximately 29% of patients with intractable bleeding treated with a single arterial embolization procedure have recurrent bleeding, most of which can be conservatively managed.
Application of ice to the neck decreases blood volume at the septum but does not improve clinical outcomes.
Having the patient with epistaxis wear a surgical mask reduces contamination of healthcare personnel by blood when the patient coughs.
Hemodynamically unstable patients should be hospitalized.
Consider hospitalizing elderly patients, patients with coagulopathy, and those with posterior packing.
Septal perforation is a potential complication of cauterization or packing. Referral is warranted if this occurs. Packing can also be complicated by infection.
Although patients with nosebleeds tend to have short-term recurrences, long-term resolution is common. B

In a prospective study of 100 consecutive adult patients, the 47 patients with a posterior bleeding site were more likely to require nasal packing, be admitted to the hospital, and have longer hospital stays.
Almost two-thirds of children referred for recurrent nosebleeds report having continued problems with nosebleeds 5 years later. B
Short-term treatment with antiseptic cream is useful, although most children will still have nosebleeds 5 years later.
Petroleum jelly does not prevent recurrence in children.
The optimal management of recurrent nosebleeds in children is unknown.

cell.label: Patient with epistaxis. Stable vital signs?

First aid: Pinch the whole nonbony portion of the nose firmly for 15 min; tilt head forward to decrease drainage of blood down the throat. If unsuccessful, blow nose, spray with decongestant, and pinch again. Still bleeding?

Cautery: Look for source of bleeding. Clear view with suction, saline lavage, decongestant. Take safety precautions to avoid contamination of personnel with blood. If discrete source is seen, selectively cauterize with silver nitrate or electrocautery. Do not blindly or excessively cauterize. Still bleeding?

Evaluation: If diffuse or unclear source of bleeding, consider systemic causes (CBC, coagulants, consider T&C), and treat causes. If coagulopathy or anticoagulants, consider fresh frozen plasma, platelets, vitamin K.

Anterior packing: Topical analgesia with 4% cocaine, lidocaine, or tetracaine. Insert nasal tampon lubricated with antibiotic ointment or pack the anterior nasal cavity with petroleum jelly-impregnated gauze. Still bleeding?
Posterior packing: Insertion of a commercial nasal catheter or insertion of a trimmed Foley catheter or consider hot-water irrigation. Still bleeding?
Surgical treatment: Selective endovascular embolization or surgical ligation of maxillary, sphenopalatine, or anterior ethmoidal artery.
Prevention of recurrence: Moisturize ambient air, antibiotic ointment in nose, avoid nasal trauma (picking, nose-blowing, closed-mouth sneezing), and teach first aid measures.
Appropriate resuscitative and stabilizing measures, including IV fluids, laboratory tests, and blood.
